sections.html:
Hopkins County splits the work between the PVA and the Sheriff. The PVA's staff lists every taxable parcel, measures and photographs buildings, values each one and builds the tax roll that the public may inspect. The office is in the Courthouse Annex, 25 East Center Street, Madisonville, KY 42431, telephone (270) 821-3092.

Billing and collection sit with the Sheriff's Office at 261 Responders Lane, phone 270-821-5661, open to taxpayers on weekdays from eight to four. Bills still open after April 15 belong to the Hopkins County Clerk, reachable at 270-326-2097.

Bills are written to the name on the parcel as of January 1. If you bought in spring, the old owner may still be receiving it and should forward it. The Sheriff can't see new deeds, so a buyer who hears nothing can ring the office or print a copy online.

Bills normally go out about September 30, and the counter opens October 1. The Sheriff runs four stages through April 15.

Yearly tax collection stages at the Hopkins County Sheriff
Payment windowWhat changes
October 1 to November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to January 315 percent added
February 1 to April 1521 percent added

Call the Sheriff for an exact payoff before paying in February or March, since fees and commission can change the total.

Sheriff collection stops when business closes on April 15, and whatever is left moves to the Clerk.

The office takes online and counter payments, and it insists on the whole amount. A partial payment is turned down.

  • Accepted: cash, personal checks, money orders, cashier's checks and cards.
  • An outside processor runs cards and charges 2.5 percent plus 30 cents.
  • Online checks cost $1.50 to process.
  • Write checks to Hopkins County Sheriff.

Escrow doesn't lift the owner's duty. The taxpayer must get the bill to the mortgage lender, and a lender can't pay what it never receives.

The bill math is taxable assessment divided by 100, times the rate set for the year. Volunteer fire department fees or watershed taxes, where they apply, are added separately.

For a sale, the Sheriff suggests a simple split. Divide the last year's bill by 365 for a daily cost, then multiply by the number of days the seller lived in the house.

Some closing agents wait for the real bill. Compare their number with the Sheriff's method before you sign the settlement statement, and ask which year's bill each of you used. If the real bill is not out yet at closing, agree in writing on the estimate and who will settle any difference. A line in the contract is enough.

Start with the PVA's office. Under KRS 133.120, a conference with the PVA or a deputy has to come first, before or during the inspection period, and you can ask to hold it by telephone.

  • The PVA walks through how the number was set and writes up the meeting.
  • If that fails, send the County Clerk a letter or petition no later than one workday after inspection closes.
  • Name the value you think is fair and back it up with land and building descriptions, insurance, cost records, listings, comparable sales or loan papers.
  • Show up for the hearing, personally or through an authorized representative.

The board may reject an appeal if you hold back information it reasonably asks for. Meanwhile, pay on the figure you claimed. Bring photos or an appraisal if you have one, and keep notes from the PVA conference, because the clerk and the board will want to know what was already discussed.

A homeowner aged 65 or older, or totally disabled, who lives in the property can deduct $49,100 from the assessment for the 2025 and 2026 years. File the form at the PVA office with proof of age, most often a birth certificate or driver's license. Disability applicants must document benefits received from January through December.

Farmland is treated differently. KRS 132.010 values agricultural land by its production capability, and qualifying land means parcels of 10 acres or more used to raise livestock or grow crops, including timber. Nobody can claim more than one exemption on one property within one county and state.

sections.h2: When the Clerk takes over a tax debt
sections.html:
Once the Clerk holds the bill, it becomes a certificate of delinquency, and a lien is entered against the property. Selling the house doesn't remove it.

The Clerk holds the tax sale electronically each fall, and buyers register at the Clerk's office, 24 Union Street, Madisonville. Buyers pay $5 per priority bill or $10 per current-year bill, capped at $250 in combined fees, and the clerk sets the payment deadline at the sale.

A buyer of a certificate can load its own fees on the account, so clearing the bill with the Sheriff before the deadline, or with the Clerk afterward, costs less. Call the Clerk for current amounts.

Hopkins County is in western Kentucky, with Madisonville as county seat and largest city. Population was 45,127 in 2025, down 0.6 percent from 2020. Owners live in 70.7 percent of homes, and 18,397 households average 2.40 people each.

The middle owned-home value is $142,800 and median gross rent is $837. Median household income is $56,815. Persons 65 or older make up 21.0 percent of the population, so homestead claims are common. Builders took out 201 permits in 2025.

Monthly owner costs run $1,107 with a mortgage and $436 without, a useful figure when a buyer weighs your price against renting.

Before you list, find out which office holds your bill. In the fall and winter it sits with the Sheriff, and after April 15 it sits with the Clerk. Ask for a written payoff from whichever one has it, and give a copy to the title company.

At closing, the title agent pays the tax from your proceeds and the buyer's lender expects the lien to clear. If you are selling for cash and want to close quickly, the payoff is the one number you can't skip, so request it a week or two ahead and ask how long it stays good.

Keep your payment receipt and the Sheriff's or Clerk's confirmation with the sale file. Also check whether a homestead deduction is on the account. It ends with your ownership, and the buyer has to apply on their own if they qualify.

faqs.q: What day does the Hopkins County discount period begin?
faqs.a: Collection opens October 1, after bills go out around September 30. Paying through November 1 earns 2 percent off, and face value applies from November 2 to year end.

faqs.q: Will Hopkins County let me split a bill into pieces?
faqs.a: No. The Sheriff takes the whole amount only and refuses part payments. Cards, cash and checks all work, and cards carry a processor fee.

faqs.q: I closed last month and received no bill. Who do I call?
faqs.a: Call the Sheriff at 270-821-5661. Bills are issued to the January 1 owner and the office does not see new deeds, so a copy can be printed from the Sheriff's website.

faqs.q: Whom do I pay once April 15 has gone by?
faqs.a: Pay the Hopkins County Clerk at 270-326-2097, since open bills go there when April 15 ends.

faqs.q: Do older owners get any relief?
faqs.a: Yes: a $49,100 homestead exemption, filed at the PVA's office on East Center Street. Owners 65 and over who live in the house qualify, as do totally disabled owners.
